en: Sutta Nipāta 1.4 Kasibhāradvājasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Dakkhiṇāgiri, in the brahmin village of Ekanālā.
Now at that time, about five hundred ploughs belonging to the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja were being yoked for the sowing season.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to where the work of the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja was being carried out.
Now at that time, the distribution of food was taking place for the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja.
Then the Blessed One approached the place where the food was being distributed; having approached, he stood to one side.
The brahmin Kasībhāradvāja saw the Blessed One standing there for alms.
Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“I, ascetic, plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat. You too, ascetic, should plow and sow; having plowed and sown, you should eat.”
“I too, brahmin, plough and sow; having ploughed and sown, I eat.
“But we do not see Master Gotama’s yoke, or plough, or ploughshare, or goad, or oxen.
And yet Master Gotama says this:”
“Brahmin, I too plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat.
Then the brahmin Kassapa Bhāradvāja addressed the Blessed One in verse: “You claim to be a farmer, yet you do not see the plow.”
Yet we do not see your plowing;
being asked about your plowing,
tell us how we may come to know your plowing.
Faith is the seed, austerity the rain,
wisdom my yoke and plough;
modesty is the pole, mind the yoke-tie.
I possess a plough for tilling;
I am guarded in body, guarded in speech,
and restrained regarding food in my belly.
Truth is my bed;
gentleness is my release;
energy is my yoke and burden.
Bringing about the security of yoga,
it goes on without turning back,
having gone where one does not grieve.
Thus this plowing has been done;
it bears the fruit of the Deathless.
Having plowed this plowing, one is not born again in a womb.
“He is liberated from all suffering.
Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja, having filled a large bronze bowl with milk-rice, offered it to the Blessed One, saying:
“May the venerable Gotama eat the milk-rice.”
“You are a farmer, sir,
for you, Master Gotama, plow the field that has the fruit of the Deathless.
“What is sung to me in verse is not food for me.”
This is not the Dhamma for those who see clearly, O Brahmin;
the Buddhas reject verses sung as praise.
When the Dhamma exists, O Brahmin, this is the proper way of life.
And with food and drink, serve the Great Sage who is perfected, whose taints are exhausted, and whose remorse has been stilled.
"For that field belongs to one who seeks merit.
"Then to whom, Master Gotama, shall I give this milk-rice?
"I do not see anyone, brahmin, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among the generation of recluses and brahmins, including gods and humans, [to whom I could give it]."
“In this generation with its devas and humans, there is no one other than a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata for whom that milk-rice, once eaten, would be properly digested.
Therefore, brahmin, either discard that milk-rice where there is no greenery, or cast it into water devoid of living beings.”
Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja threw that milk-rice into water devoid of living beings.
As soon as that milk-rice was thrown into the water, it hissed, sizzled, smoked, and billowed with smoke.
It was just like a ploughshare heated all day that, when thrown into water, hisses, sizzles, smokes, and billows with smoke.
In the same way, that milk-rice, when thrown into the water, hissed and sizzled, smoked and billowed.

Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja, stirred with emotion and his hair standing on end, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he prostrated himself at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!”
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost,
or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms— in the same way,
the Dhamma has been made clear by Master Gotama through many lines of reasoning."
“I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of Master Gotama; may I receive the full ordination.
Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received the full ordination.
Not long after his full ordination, the Venerable Bhāradvāja, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,

in no long time realized for himself through direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; and having attained it, he dwelt therein.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the fourth sutta, the Kasibhāradvājasutta.
